title: Ask a Better Question
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Asking great questions is described as a scarce skill and the most valuable tool in a leader's kit. Good questions need not be clever; they only have to get others talking, which builds trust and guides people to what they are missing. The author's core rule is that when a leader dislikes an answer, the fault lies in the question rather than the responder. He gives a concrete example: replacing How was your day with What was the best thing that happened today. Learning to craft better questions takes trial and error, but better questions reliably get better answers.
points: Questions build trust and let leaders guide people rather than tell them.
Great questions are simple and expansive, designed to get others talking.
The rule is that a disappointing answer signals a flawed question, not a flawed responder.
Swapping How was your day for What was the best thing that happened today shows the principle in practice.
quotes: The benefits of great questions go beyond expanding knowledge and gaining insight. Well-constructed questions can build trust and rapport with others and guide them to, rather than tell them, what they are missing. Of the many tools of leadership, great questions are unequaled in their value and impact.
Great questions don’t have to be complex or clever or brilliant. They simply have to get others talking. The power of a superbly crafted question to get people to share their views is amazing.

Like many things leadership, learning from others through questions is more about the questioner than the answerer. Whenever good leaders don't like the answer to a question they pose, they know it's due to the question, not the responder.
The rule good leaders live by is this: If I don’t like the answer, I need to ask a better question.

Asking someone, “How was your day?” may elicit a wide variety of responses, including the lazy reply of, “Fine.” In the eyes of a good leader, this is more a function of the question than it is the responder. Ask a better question, such as, “What was the best thing that happened today?” Suddenly, the other person begins to talk.
They soon appreciate it is not the answer that illuminates what people think, but the question that breaks down the door. Better questions get better answers.
